walkthroughs.body_html: River Eden drains 2400 km^2 of Cumbria. Steep relief and impermeable Carboniferous rocks produce flashy hydrograph. Mean annual discharge 50 cumecs but storm peaks exceed 1700 cumecs. Land use includes upland grazing, lowland farming, urban Penrith and Carlisle.

Honister Pass received 341 mm in 24 hours (UK record). Atmospheric river fuelled by Atlantic moisture. Eden rose 7.7 m at Sheepmount, Carlisle. Insurers paid £1.3 billion in claims. 5200 homes flooded across Cumbria; 7000 businesses affected.

Hard engineering: Carlisle £25 million flood walls (post-2005 floods). Soft: tree planting upstream (Cumbria Woodlands project), peatland restoration, river restoration to reduce flow speed. Stroud rural sustainable drainage uses leaky dams. Combining strategies reflects modern integrated approach.

options: It is the process of rain falling from clouds.
The time between peak rainfall and peak river discharge — affected by drainage basin shape, land use, soil saturation and vegetation.
Lag time is how long the storm itself lasts.
Lag time is the delay between thunder and lightning.
It is only water evaporating from puddles and lakes.
Humans affect the carbon cycle by eating plants.
It is the process of rain falling from clouds.
The combined loss of water from a surface through evaporation (from soil and water bodies) and transpiration (from plant leaves).

mcqs.q: How do humans affect the carbon cycle?
options: Lag time is the delay between thunder and lightning.
By burning fossil fuels (releasing stored geological carbon to the atmosphere) and deforestation (reducing the biosphere store and releasing carbon).
Humans affect the carbon cycle by eating plants.
Humans only affect the carbon cycle by breathing out CO2.
